rv.q: Jane Alexander and James Cromwell deliver a miniature master class in the art of slyly ambiguous acting
The Sparkle and Glow of 'Grand Horizons'

Bill and Nancy, the husband and wife at the heart of this new play by Bess Wohl, fall into the latter category. As Grand Horizons begins, they are performing a brittle pas de deux around the salt shaker in advance of what promises to be a mirthlessly taciturn dinner in a bland suburban retirement community.
Grand Horizons is not especially profound, and its women are written more fully than its men.
Once past the unfortunate opening scenes, suggesting that the play might center on the superficial Brian, the focus shifts to Nancy and Bill and this smartly constructed comedy finds its footing.
For those few minutes, at least, Grand Horizons achieves a poignancy and depth that have otherwise eluded it.
Best efforts and a sweet heart notwithstanding, Grand Horizons falls short of its expansive title.
Bess Wohl's 'Grand Horizons,' which is, by contrast, only just funny enough.

Unfortunately, her realization that she can no longer tell the requisite wifely lies — the ones that say her husband and children are infinitely excusable — comes too late in her life, as too late in the play.

Michael Urie, Ashley Park, Ben McKenzie, Priscilla Lopez co-star in Leigh Silverman's production. Back in that age we call golden, Broadway marquees were frequently set ablaze by long-running plays that producers looking to turn a profit lovingly referred to as boulevard comedies.

Theater seems to be single-handedly attempting to revive the boulevard comedy on Broadway. There was a time when the Great White Way was dominated by such middlebrow, mass-appeal fare, with the late, great Neil Simon as the chief avatar of the genre.
The comedy and drama in Grand Horizons work in clever interplay.
It’s damn funny, and very on-point.
Back and forth the play goes—sometimes silly, sometimes deadly serious.
But the play’s horizons are too easy and narrow.
With Grand Horizons, she seems to have wanted to step back and try her hand at a traditional, non-challenging, old-fashioned sex comedy.

cn.t: Wohl's Neil Simon-esque comedy about late-life divorce earns mostly positive reviews for its stellar cast led by Alexander and Cromwell, though critics find the writing familiar and middlebrow, straining between sitcom laughs and deeper insights.
